name: McLaren Vale
summary: Mediterranean-climate region south of Adelaide between the Mount Lofty Ranges and Gulf St Vincent, home to some of Australia's oldest Grenache and Shiraz vines and a leader in sustainable and alternative-variety viticulture.
climate: Warm Mediterranean, moderated by sea breezes from the gulf; dry summers and winter rainfall.
soils: Exceptionally varied geology, from ancient Cambrian schist and quartzite to sand over clay, terra rossa, ironstone and limestone; mapped as 19 distinct districts.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Mourvèdre, plus a growing range of Mediterranean grapes such as Fiano, Vermentino, Tempranillo and Nero d'Avola.

name: South Australia
summary: State-level designation for wines blended across several South Australian regions. The state makes around half of Australia's wine.
climate: Ranges from hot inland irrigated areas to cool, elevated and maritime regions in the Adelaide Hills and Limestone Coast.
soils: Diverse: red-brown earths, terra rossa over limestone, sandy loams and ironstone; phylloxera-free, so many vineyards are on their own roots.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Barossa Valley
summary: Australia's best-known wine region, settled by Silesian Lutherans in the 1840s, with some of the world's oldest continuously producing Shiraz, Grenache and Mourvèdre vines.
climate: Warm and dry continental, with hot summer days and cool nights; low rainfall makes old dry-grown vines prized.
soils: Varied red-brown earths, sandy loams and grey-brown clays over limestone and ironstone; deep sand in the north-west.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Grenache, Mourvèdre (Mataro), Cabernet Sauvignon, Semillon.
blends: GSM, Shiraz–Cabernet; fortified Tawny and Apera traditions.

name: Adelaide Hills
summary: Elevated, cool region in the Mount Lofty Ranges just east of Adelaide; South Australia's go-to source for crisp whites, sparkling base and elegant reds.
climate: Cool to moderate, with altitude (400–700 m) driving long ripening, cool nights and higher rainfall than the plains.
soils: Sandy loams and clay over weathered schist, sandstone and ironstone.
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Shiraz, Grüner Veltliner, Gamay.
blends: Traditional-method sparkling (Chardonnay–Pinot Noir); cool-climate Shiraz often co-fermented with Viognier.

name: Clare Valley
summary: A series of narrow north–south valleys north of Adelaide, famous for bone-dry, lime-scented Riesling that ages for decades, especially from the Watervale and Polish Hill sub-regions.
climate: Continental with warm days and markedly cool nights, plus elevation (300–500 m) that preserves acidity.
soils: Terra rossa over limestone (Watervale) and slate and shale (Polish Hill), with red-brown loams elsewhere.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Malbec.
blends: Cabernet–Malbec is a regional speciality; also Shiraz–Cabernet.

name: Langhorne Creek
summary: Flat, fertile region on the Bremer and Angas river floodplains near Lake Alexandrina, a key supplier of soft, generous reds to many South Australian blends.
climate: Moderate maritime, cooled by the 'Lake Doctor' breeze off Lake Alexandrina.
soils: Deep alluvial sandy and clay loams, historically flood-irrigated by winter floods.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Malbec, Petit Verdot, Merlot, Montepulciano.
blends: Cabernet–Shiraz and Cabernet–Malbec blends; components for multi-regional labels.

name: Coonawarra
summary: A narrow 27 km cigar-shaped strip on the Limestone Coast, renowned for structured, mint- and cassis-tinged Cabernet Sauvignon grown on its famous red soil.
climate: Cool maritime, influenced by Southern Ocean winds; long, even ripening with frost risk in spring.
soils: Terra rossa: a thin band of red, iron-rich clay loam over limestone and a high water table.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Chardonnay, Riesling.

name: Yarra Valley
summary: Victoria's first wine region, just north-east of Melbourne, producing elegant, finely structured Chardonnay and Pinot Noir and a strong sparkling tradition.
climate: Cool, with marked variation from the warmer valley floor to the cold, higher Upper Yarra.
soils: Grey sandy clay loams over sandstone on the valley floor; deep red volcanic soils in the Upper Yarra.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Nebbiolo.
blends: Traditional-method sparkling; Bordeaux-style Cabernet blends; Shiraz–Viognier.

name: Riverland
summary: South Australia's largest-volume region along the Murray River, the engine room of affordable Australian wine and an increasingly interesting source of alternative varieties.
climate: Hot, dry continental with high sunshine; relies on Murray River irrigation.
soils: Red sandy loams and calcareous sands over limestone.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, plus Fiano, Montepulciano, Nero d'Avola and Vermentino.
blends: Value red and white blends; components for South Eastern Australia labels.

name: Eden Valley
summary: The elevated, rugged eastern neighbour of the Barossa (part of the Barossa zone), producing taut, floral Riesling and finely spiced Shiraz, including some of Australia's most famous single vineyards.
climate: Cool for South Australia thanks to altitude (380–550 m); later ripening than the Barossa floor.
soils: Thin, rocky, acidic soils of weathered schist, quartz and ironstone.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier.
blends: Mostly varietal wines; Eden Valley fruit is often blended into Barossa Shiraz.

name: Margaret River
summary: Western Australia's flagship region on a peninsula between two oceans, producing a large share of Australia's premium Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
climate: Maritime Mediterranean, the most marine-influenced in Australia; warm, dry summers and mild winters.
soils: Gravelly and sandy loams over granite and gneiss; ironstone gravels prized for Cabernet.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Merlot, Shiraz.

name: Southern Fleurieu
summary: Small, cool region at the southern tip of the Fleurieu Peninsula, between McLaren Vale and Cape Jervis, best known for brisk whites and medium-bodied reds.
climate: Cool maritime, exposed to Southern Ocean and gulf winds.
soils: Sandy loams and podzolic soils over ironstone and weathered schist.
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Victoria
summary: State-level designation for wines blended across Victorian regions. Victoria has more wine regions than any other state, from the cool south coast to the warm north-east.
climate: From cool maritime (Mornington, Geelong) and alpine (Macedon) to warm inland (Rutherglen, Murray Darling).
soils: Very varied: volcanic basalts, granite-derived sands, ancient sedimentary and alluvial soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling, Muscat.
blends: Cross-regional Shiraz and sparkling; Rutherglen Muscat and Topaque fortifieds.

name: Tasmania
summary: Australia's coolest wine state, island-wide a single GI, now the country's benchmark for sparkling wine and a fast-rising source of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Riesling.
climate: Cool maritime, with long, mild growing seasons and high natural acidity.
soils: Dolerite- and basalt-derived soils, sandstone, mudstone and river gravels, varying by valley (Tamar, Coal River, Derwent, Huon).
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris.
blends: Traditional-method sparkling from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

name: Grampians
summary: Western Victorian region at the foot of the Grampians ranges, centred on Great Western, with a long history of spicy, peppery cool-climate Shiraz and sparkling Shiraz.
climate: Cool to moderate continental, with significant altitude and diurnal range.
soils: Grey-brown sandy loams over clay, and weathered sandstone and granite.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Meunier.

name: Great Western
summary: Historic sub-region of the Grampians, home to Seppelt and Best's since the 1860s and some of Victoria's oldest Shiraz vines; birthplace of Australian sparkling Shiraz.
climate: Cool continental with low rainfall; frost and drought are the main risks.
soils: Grey-brown loamy sands over clay and decomposed granite.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Riesling, Pinot Meunier, Chardonnay.
blends: Sparkling Shiraz; field-blend plantings in old nurseries.

name: Geelong
summary: Cool maritime region on Port Phillip Bay's western side, including the Bellarine Peninsula and Moorabool Valley, known for intense, mineral Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Shiraz.
climate: Cool, dry and windy maritime, with low rainfall and small yields.
soils: Black cracking volcanic clays over limestone (Moorabool) and sandy loams on the Bellarine.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling.

name: Murray Darling
summary: Large, irrigated region straddling the Murray River between Victoria and New South Wales, around Mildura; a major source of everyday Australian wine.
climate: Hot, sunny and dry continental; dependent on river irrigation.
soils: Red-brown sandy loams and calcareous sands (Mallee soils).
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, plus alternative grapes such as Fiano, Nero d'Avola and Lagrein.
blends: Value blends and components for South Eastern Australia labels.

name: New South Wales
summary: State-level designation for wines blended across New South Wales regions, from the historic Hunter Valley to the high country of Orange and the irrigated Riverina.
climate: Humid subtropical (Hunter), cool elevated (Orange, Tumbarumba), hot inland (Riverina).
soils: Varied: alluvial loams, volcanic basalt, and red-brown earths.
typical_varietals: Semillon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon.
blends: Cross-regional reds; Riverina botrytis Semillon dessert wines.

name: Heathcote
summary: Central Victorian region along the Mount Camel Range, famous for deep, plush yet savoury Shiraz grown on ancient red Cambrian soil.
climate: Warm continental, moderated by the range's altitude and cooling southerly winds.
soils: Deep red Cambrian greenstone soil (weathered volcanic rock over 500 million years old).
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Nebbiolo, Tempranillo, Sangiovese.

name: Wrattonbully
summary: Limestone Coast region just north of Coonawarra, planted mostly since the 1990s, producing well-structured Cabernet, Shiraz and Merlot.
climate: Cool to moderate maritime with good air drainage on gentle slopes, reducing frost risk.
soils: Terra rossa and sandy loams over limestone, similar to Coonawarra.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Tempranillo, Chardonnay.
blends: Cabernet–Merlot; often blended with Coonawarra fruit.

name: Great Southern
summary: Western Australia's largest and coolest region, with five sub-regions (Albany, Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker, Porongurup); known for intense Riesling and peppery Shiraz.
climate: Cool maritime near the coast and more continental inland, with long, slow ripening.
soils: Lateritic gravelly loams and sandy soils over ancient granite.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

name: Padthaway
summary: Limestone Coast region north of Coonawarra, established in the 1960s, supplying quality Chardonnay and Shiraz to many large producers.
climate: Moderate maritime, slightly warmer than Coonawarra.
soils: Terra rossa and brown sandy loams over limestone.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

name: Alpine Valleys
summary: North-east Victorian region of river valleys (Ovens, Kiewa, Buffalo, Buckland) beneath the Victorian Alps, with a strong Italian-variety tradition.
climate: Cool to warm depending on altitude, with cold nights and high rainfall.
soils: Alluvial and granitic soils on valley floors, red loams on slopes.
typical_varietals: Prosecco (Glera), Tempranillo, Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay.

name: Pyrenees
summary: Central Victorian region around Avoca and Moonambel, known for robust, minty Shiraz and Cabernet and some sparkling.
climate: Moderate continental with cool nights from altitude.
soils: Grey-brown loams and sandy soils over clay, with quartz gravels.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: King Valley
summary: North-east Victorian valley settled by Italian families, the Australian home of Prosecco and other Italian varieties.
climate: Ranges from warm on the valley floor to cool at Whitlands (up to 800 m).
soils: Red and grey loams, alluvial soils on the valley floor.
typical_varietals: Prosecco (Glera), Pinot Grigio, Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Barbera, Riesling.

name: Macedon Ranges
summary: Mainland Australia's coolest wine region, north-west of Melbourne, producing taut sparkling wine, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
climate: Very cool and windy continental, with altitude up to 800 m; ripening can be marginal.
soils: Granite-derived sandy soils and volcanic basalt loams.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Shiraz.

name: Goulburn Valley
summary: Central Victorian region along the Goulburn River, including the Nagambie Lakes sub-region, home to Tahbilk's 1860 Shiraz and the world's largest Marsanne plantings.
climate: Warm continental, moderated by the river and lakes around Nagambie.
soils: Red sandy loams with high iron content and alluvial river soils.
typical_varietals: Marsanne, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Roussanne, Viognier.

name: Hunter Valley
summary: Australia's oldest continuously operating wine region, north of Sydney, famous for low-alcohol, long-lived Semillon and medium-bodied, earthy Shiraz.
climate: Warm, humid subtropical, with summer rain and cloud cover during vintage.
soils: Sandy alluvial flats (best for Semillon) and red volcanic and clay loams on slopes (Shiraz).
typical_varietals: Semillon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Verdelho.
blends: Mostly varietal; historic 'Hunter Burgundy' Shiraz–Pinot styles.

name: Mudgee
summary: Elevated region on the western slopes of the Great Dividing Range in New South Wales, known for rich reds and Chardonnay.
climate: Warm continental with altitude (450–1,100 m) and cold nights.
soils: Sandy loams over clay, with some volcanic soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Barbera.

name: Orange
summary: High-altitude New South Wales region on the slopes of the extinct volcano Mount Canobolas, defined by a minimum altitude of 600 m.
climate: Cool continental from altitude; frost and snow are possible.
soils: Red-brown basalt-derived volcanic soils and limestone.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Canberra District
summary: Cool region surrounding the national capital, best known for Shiraz co-fermented with Viognier and for Riesling.
climate: Cool continental with cold winters and hot, dry summer days.
soils: Shallow granitic and shale soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

name: Rutherglen
summary: North-east Victorian region famous for luscious fortified Muscat and Topaque (Muscadelle), aged for decades in old barrels.
climate: Hot continental, with long, dry autumns ideal for raisining fruit.
soils: Red loams and sandy alluvial soils.
typical_varietals: Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge, Muscadelle (Topaque), Durif, Shiraz.
blends: Fortified Muscat and Topaque, graded Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare.

name: Mornington Peninsula
summary: Maritime peninsula south of Melbourne surrounded by water on three sides, producing elegant Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris.
climate: Cool maritime, moderated by Port Phillip and Western Port bays.
soils: Red volcanic soils, brown duplex soils and sandy loams.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Shiraz.

name: Beechworth
summary: Small, elevated north-east Victorian region with a cult following for complex Chardonnay and savoury Shiraz.
climate: Cool to moderate continental with altitude.
soils: Granite-derived gravels and some ancient shale and sandstone.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Nebbiolo, Sangiovese.

name: Frankland River
summary: The most northerly and inland sub-region of Great Southern, noted for perfumed Riesling and structured Shiraz and Cabernet.
climate: Cool continental, dry and with a large diurnal range.
soils: Gravelly lateritic loams over granite and gneiss.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec.

name: Kangaroo Island
summary: South Australia's island region off the Fleurieu Peninsula, with a small number of producers making maritime-influenced reds and whites.
climate: Cool maritime, with constant ocean breezes.
soils: Sandy loams over ironstone and limestone.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.

name: Aconcagua
summary: Region north of Santiago named after the Americas' highest peak, including the cool coastal Casablanca and San Antonio valleys and the warmer inland Aconcagua Valley.
climate: Warm inland, cooled by the Andes at night; coastal sub-regions are cool from the Humboldt Current.
soils: Alluvial and colluvial gravels inland; granite and clay on the coast.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Carmenère, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir (coastal).

name: Central Valley
summary: Chile's heartland of wine production between the Andes and the Coastal Range, including the Maipo, Rapel (Colchagua, Cachapoal), Curicó and Maule valleys.
climate: Warm Mediterranean with dry summers and a large diurnal range from Andes breezes.
soils: Alluvial gravels and loams, with granite in the Coastal Range.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, País, Carignan.
blends: Cabernet–Carmenère; old-vine Carignan blends (VIGNO) in Maule.

name: Shandong
summary: Coastal province on the Yellow Sea and one of China's oldest modern wine regions, centred on Yantai and Penglai, where Changyu was founded in 1892.
climate: Monsoonal maritime: humid with summer rain, which brings disease pressure.
soils: Sandy loams and granite-derived soils.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Gernischt (Carmenère), Merlot, Marselan, Chardonnay.

name: Rhone
summary: The Rhône Valley runs from Vienne to Avignon, with the steep, Syrah-dominated Northern Rhône (Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage) and the broader, Grenache-led Southern Rhône (Châteauneuf-du-Pape).
climate: Continental in the north; Mediterranean in the south, shaped by the cold Mistral wind.
soils: Granite and schist slopes in the north; galets roulés (large round stones), limestone, sand and clay in the south.
typical_varietals: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier, Marsanne, Roussanne, Cinsault.
blends: Southern Rhône GSM blends (Châteauneuf-du-Pape permits 13 grapes); Northern Syrah co-fermented with Viognier.

name: Bordeaux
summary: The world's benchmark for blended reds, along the Gironde estuary and Garonne and Dordogne rivers, divided into the Left Bank (Médoc, Graves) and Right Bank (Saint-Émilion, Pomerol).
climate: Temperate maritime, moderated by the Atlantic and the Landes forest; vintage variation is significant.
soils: Gravel over clay on the Left Bank (Cabernet); clay and limestone on the Right Bank (Merlot).
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon.
blends: Left Bank Cabernet–Merlot, Right Bank Merlot–Cabernet Franc, white Sauvignon–Semillon, and botrytised Sauternes.

name: Savoie
summary: Alpine region in eastern France near the Swiss and Italian borders, making crisp, light mountain wines from local grapes.
climate: Cool continental and alpine, moderated by lakes (Bourget, Geneva).
soils: Limestone scree, glacial moraine and molasse.
typical_varietals: Jacquère, Altesse (Roussette), Bergeron (Roussanne), Mondeuse, Gamay.
blends: Mostly varietal; Crémant de Savoie sparkling.

name: Loire Valley
summary: France's longest river runs through a string of diverse regions, from Muscadet near the Atlantic through Anjou and Touraine to Sancerre in the east.
climate: Maritime in the west, becoming more continental eastwards; cool overall.
soils: Granite and schist (Muscadet), tuffeau limestone (Touraine, Saumur), flint and Kimmeridgian marl (Sancerre).
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc, Melon de Bourgogne, Gamay.
blends: Crémant de Loire; Anjou rosé; mostly varietal still wines.

name: Languedoc-Roussillon
summary: A vast Mediterranean arc from the Rhône delta to the Spanish border, transformed from bulk wine to a source of characterful value and old-vine wines.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean with strong winds (Tramontane, Mistral).
soils: Schist, limestone, gravel terraces and clay; Roussillon has black schist.
typical_varietals: Grenache, Syrah, Carignan, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Picpoul, Grenache Blanc.
blends: GSM-plus-Carignan reds; Vins Doux Naturels such as Banyuls and Maury; Crémant de Limoux.

name: Alsace
summary: Long, narrow strip on the foothills of the Vosges mountains bordering Germany, known for aromatic, often varietally labelled whites.
climate: Sunny and dry continental: the Vosges rain shadow makes it one of France's driest regions.
soils: An extremely varied mosaic of granite, limestone, schist, sandstone, volcanic and marl soils across 51 Grand Crus.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir.
blends: Edelzwicker and Gentil field blends; Crémant d'Alsace; late-harvest Vendanges Tardives.

name: Bourgogne
summary: Burgundy, the spiritual home of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, where wine is classified by climat (vineyard plot), from regional to Premier and Grand Cru.
climate: Cool continental, with frost and hail risks; ripening varies a lot between vintages.
soils: Jurassic limestone and marl on the east-facing Côte d'Or slopes; Kimmeridgian clay in Chablis.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Aligoté, Gamay.
blends: Almost always single-varietal; Crémant de Bourgogne.

name: Champagne
summary: The northernmost major French region, around Reims and Épernay, where traditional-method sparkling wine reached its benchmark form.
climate: Cool and marginal continental with Atlantic influence; still wines are naturally high in acid.
soils: Chalk subsoil (porous, retains water, reflects heat) under thin topsoil; marl and clay in the Aube.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier.
blends: Non-vintage house blends across grapes, villages and years; Blanc de Blancs and Blanc de Noirs.

name: Beaujolais
summary: Gamay country south of Burgundy, from fresh Beaujolais Nouveau to structured wines from its ten Crus such as Morgon, Fleurie and Moulin-à-Vent.
climate: Semi-continental with Mediterranean influence from the south.
soils: Pink granite in the northern Crus; clay and limestone in the south.
typical_varietals: Gamay, Chardonnay.
blends: Single-varietal Gamay, often made by carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration.

name: Provence
summary: Sun-soaked south-eastern region between the Rhône and the Riviera, the world's reference for pale, dry rosé.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean with the Mistral wind.
soils: Limestone in the west and crystalline schist and granite in the east.
typical_varietals: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Rolle (Vermentino), Tibouren.

name: Nahe
summary: Small region along the Nahe river between the Mosel and Rheinhessen, producing some of Germany's most expressive Riesling from a mosaic of volcanic and slate soils.
climate: Cool continental, sheltered by the Hunsrück hills; dry and sunny for Germany.
soils: A highly varied mix of volcanic porphyry, slate, quartzite, sandstone and loess.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Silvaner, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir.

name: Franconia
summary: Franken, in northern Bavaria along the Main river, famous for dry, earthy Silvaner sold in the squat flagon-shaped Bocksbeutel bottle.
climate: Continental, with cold winters, frost risk and warm, dry summers.
soils: Muschelkalk (shell limestone), Keuper marl and red sandstone.
typical_varietals: Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau, Bacchus, Riesling, Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir).

name: Mosel
summary: Germany's best-known region, where vines cling to precipitous slate slopes above the winding Mosel, Saar and Ruwer rivers, producing delicate, low-alcohol Riesling.
climate: Cool and marginal; the river and steep south-facing slopes are crucial for ripening.
soils: Blue and red Devonian slate, which retains heat.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Elbling, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Blanc.
blends: Riesling across Prädikat sweetness levels, from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese.

name: Pfalz
summary: Germany's second-largest region, a warm, sunny extension of Alsace, known for full, dry Riesling and increasingly for Pinot Noir.
climate: One of Germany's warmest and driest, sheltered by the Haardt mountains.
soils: Sandstone, limestone, loess, loam and basalt.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Dornfelder, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Spätburgunder.
blends: Mostly varietal; VDP Grosses Gewächs dry wines.

name: Naoussa
summary: PDO in Macedonia, northern Greece, on the slopes of Mount Vermio, home of age-worthy, structured Xinomavro, often compared to Nebbiolo.
climate: Continental, with cold winters, rainfall and altitude (150–350 m).
soils: Varied clay, sand, limestone and marl.
typical_varietals: Xinomavro.
blends: PDO wines are 100% Xinomavro; regional blends with Merlot or Syrah.

name: Peloponnese
summary: Large peninsula in southern Greece that includes Nemea, home of Agiorgitiko, and Mantinia, known for floral, crisp Moschofilero.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast, becoming cooler and continental with altitude in the mountainous interior.
soils: Limestone, clay and schist, with sandy coastal soils.
typical_varietals: Agiorgitiko, Moschofilero, Roditis, Mavrodaphne.
blends: Varietal Nemea reds; sweet Mavrodaphne of Patras fortified.

name: Tuscany
summary: Central Italy's iconic region of rolling hills, home to Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano and the coastal 'Super Tuscans' of Bolgheri.
climate: Mediterranean, warm and dry on the coast; more continental and elevated inland.
soils: Galestro (friable schistous clay) and alberese (limestone) in Chianti; coastal gravels and clays in Bolgheri.
typical_varietals: Sangiovese, Canaiolo, Colorino, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Vernaccia, Trebbiano.
blends: Chianti (Sangiovese-led); Super Tuscans (Bordeaux varieties with or without Sangiovese); Vin Santo.

name: Sicily
summary: The Mediterranean's largest island, now a vibrant quality region, from the volcanic slopes of Etna to the hot western plains and Marsala.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean; Etna has cool mountain conditions at up to 1,000 m.
soils: Volcanic sands and ash on Etna; limestone, clay and sand elsewhere.
typical_varietals: Nero d'Avola, Nerello Mascalese, Frappato, Grillo, Carricante, Catarratto.
blends: Cerasuolo di Vittoria (Nero d'Avola–Frappato), Etna Rosso (Nerello Mascalese–Cappuccio), Marsala fortified.

name: Sardinia
summary: Rugged island with Spanish-influenced grapes, celebrated for Cannonau (Grenache) and crisp, saline Vermentino.
climate: Hot, dry and windy Mediterranean (the Mistral).
soils: Granite, schist, sand and limestone.
typical_varietals: Cannonau (Grenache), Vermentino, Carignano, Monica, Bovale.
blends: Mostly varietal; Carignano del Sulcis from old bush vines.

name: Puglia
summary: The heel of Italy's boot, a hot, productive region known for ripe, generous reds.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean, moderated by two seas.
soils: Red clay (terra rossa) over limestone.
typical_varietals: Primitivo, Negroamaro, Nero di Troia, Malvasia Nera.

name: Emilia-Romagna
summary: Fertile northern region spanning the Po plain, the gastronomic home of Lambrusco and of Sangiovese di Romagna.
climate: Continental with hot, humid summers and foggy winters.
soils: Alluvial plains, clay and limestone in the Apennine foothills.
typical_varietals: Lambrusco (several types), Sangiovese, Albana, Trebbiano, Pignoletto.

name: Marche
summary: Adriatic-coast region of central Italy, best known for the crisp, almond-tinged white Verdicchio.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast, continental inland.
soils: Clay, limestone and sandstone.
typical_varietals: Verdicchio, Montepulciano, Sangiovese, Pecorino, Lacrima.

name: Friuli-Venezia Giulia
summary: North-eastern region on the Slovenian border, celebrated for aromatic and textured whites and as a pioneer of skin-contact orange wine.
climate: Cool to moderate, protected from the north by the Alps and cooled by the Adriatic.
soils: Ponca (layered marl and sandstone) in Collio and Colli Orientali; gravel on the plains.
typical_varietals: Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc, Refosco, Schioppettino.
blends: White field blends; amber, skin-contact Ribolla.

name: Piemonte
summary: North-western Italy at the foot of the Alps, home of Barolo and Barbaresco (Nebbiolo) and much-loved everyday Barbera, Dolcetto and Moscato d'Asti.
climate: Continental with cold, foggy autumns (nebbia gave Nebbiolo its name).
soils: Calcareous marl and sandstone in the Langhe.
typical_varietals: Nebbiolo, Barbera, Dolcetto, Moscato, Arneis, Cortese.

name: Veneto
summary: North-eastern region including Valpolicella, Soave and Prosecco country.
climate: Continental, moderated by Lake Garda and the Adriatic.
soils: Limestone and volcanic basalt (Soave), marl and morainic soils.
typical_varietals: Corvina, Rondinella, Garganega, Glera, Pinot Grigio.
blends: Amarone and Ripasso (dried-grape Valpolicella blends); Prosecco.

name: Hawke's Bay
summary: New Zealand's oldest and second-largest region on the North Island's east coast, its leading source of Bordeaux-style reds and Syrah, especially from the Gimblett Gravels.
climate: Warm and sunny maritime, sheltered by inland ranges.
soils: Varied: free-draining Gimblett Gravels, alluvial silts, and limestone in the hills.
typical_varietals: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Marlborough
summary: New Zealand's largest region at the top of the South Island, which put the country on the map with intensely aromatic Sauvignon Blanc.
climate: Cool, sunny and dry maritime, with a large diurnal range.
soils: Stony alluvial gravels in the Wairau Valley; heavier clays in the Southern Valleys and Awatere.
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling.

name: Central Otago
summary: The world's southernmost wine region, a dramatic, mountainous area producing vibrant, concentrated Pinot Noir.
climate: Semi-continental: hot, dry summers, cold winters, frost risk and very high UV.
soils: Wind-blown loess and gravels over schist.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Chardonnay.

name: Wairarapa
summary: Small North Island region around Martinborough, near Wellington, with a reputation for savoury, structured Pinot Noir.
climate: Cool, windy maritime, with dry autumns.
soils: Free-draining alluvial gravel terraces and loess.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Syrah.

name: Duoro
summary: The Douro Valley in northern Portugal, one of the world's oldest demarcated regions (1756), home of Port and of increasingly acclaimed dry reds, grown on steep terraced slopes.
climate: Hot, dry continental, sheltered from the Atlantic by the Marão mountains.
soils: Schist, which is broken up to make terraces and lets roots go deep.
typical_varietals: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão.
blends: Port, and dry red field blends from old mixed plantings.

name: Douro
summary: One of the world's oldest demarcated regions (1756), home of Port and of increasingly acclaimed dry reds, grown on steep terraced slopes along the Douro river.
climate: Hot, dry continental, sheltered from the Atlantic by the Marão mountains.
soils: Schist, which is broken up to make terraces and lets roots go deep.
typical_varietals: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão.
blends: Port, and dry red field blends from old mixed plantings.

name: Lisboa
summary: Atlantic-facing region north of Lisbon, a source of fresh, good-value whites and reds, including the historic sub-regions of Colares and Bucelas.
climate: Maritime, cool and humid, with strong Atlantic winds.
soils: Clay and limestone, with sand dunes at Colares (where vines survived phylloxera).
typical_varietals: Arinto, Fernão Pires, Castelão, Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Ramisco.
blends: Blends of Portuguese and international grapes.

name: Stellenbosch
summary: South Africa's most famous region, east of Cape Town, with mountain slopes and valleys producing the country's finest Cabernet, Bordeaux blends and Pinotage.
climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooled by False Bay breezes and the 'Cape Doctor' wind.
soils: Decomposed granite on mountain slopes and sandstone-derived soils on valley floors.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinotage, Chenin Blanc, Syrah, Merlot, Chardonnay.

name: Valdapeñas
summary: Valdepeñas, a DO in the south of La Mancha, Castilla-La Mancha, historically supplying Madrid with soft, affordable Tempranillo (locally Cencibel).
climate: Extreme continental: very hot summers, cold winters, low rainfall.
soils: Red-brown clay over limestone, with a chalky crust.
typical_varietals: Tempranillo (Cencibel), Airén, Garnacha, Cabernet Sauvignon.
blends: Tempranillo, traditionally softened with white Airén.

name: Valdepeñas
summary: DO in the south of La Mancha, Castilla-La Mancha, historically supplying Madrid with soft, affordable Tempranillo (locally Cencibel).
climate: Extreme continental: very hot summers, cold winters, low rainfall.
soils: Red-brown clay over limestone, with a chalky crust.
typical_varietals: Tempranillo (Cencibel), Airén, Garnacha, Cabernet Sauvignon.
blends: Tempranillo, traditionally softened with white Airén.

name: Rioja
summary: Spain's most famous red region, along the Ebro river in the north, with three sub-zones (Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa, Rioja Oriental) and an ageing classification from Joven to Gran Reserva.
climate: Atlantic-influenced continental in the west, warmer and Mediterranean in the east.
soils: Calcareous clay (Alavesa, Alta), ferrous clay and alluvial soils (Oriental).
typical_varietals: Tempranillo, Garnacha, Graciano, Mazuelo (Carignan), Viura.
blends: Tempranillo-led blends with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo, traditionally aged in American oak.

name: Catalonia
summary: North-eastern Spain, home of Cava (around Penedès), the powerful old-vine reds of Priorat and Montsant, and a lively natural-wine scene.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast, more continental and elevated inland.
soils: Llicorella (slate and quartz) in Priorat; limestone and clay in Penedès.
typical_varietals: Garnacha, Cariñena (Samsó), Macabeo, Xarel·lo, Parellada, Tempranillo (Ull de Llebre).

name: Manchuela
summary: DO on the high plateau between La Mancha and Valencia, revived by producers working with old-vine Bobal.
climate: Continental with Mediterranean influence: hot days, cool nights and altitude (600–1,000 m).
soils: Limestone and clay.
typical_varietals: Bobal, Tempranillo, Garnacha Tintorera, Macabeo, Moravia Agria.

name: Ribera del Duero
summary: High-plateau region along the Duero river in Castilla y León, producing powerful, structured Tempranillo (Tinto Fino), including the legendary Vega Sicilia.
climate: Extreme continental at 750–1,000 m, with a huge diurnal range.
soils: Limestone, chalk and clay with alluvial gravels.
typical_varietals: Tempranillo (Tinto Fino), Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec.

name: Priorat
summary: One of Spain's two DOCa regions, in Catalonia, making concentrated reds from old vines on steep slate terraces.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean, moderated by altitude.
soils: Llicorella: crumbly slate and quartz.
typical_varietals: Garnacha, Cariñena, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah.
blends: Garnacha–Cariñena with Bordeaux and Rhône varieties.

name: California
summary: Produces around 80% of US wine, from the prestigious North Coast (Napa, Sonoma) through the Central Coast to the high-volume Central Valley.
climate: Mediterranean, cooled by Pacific fog along the coast; hot inland.
soils: Hugely varied: volcanic, alluvial fans, marine sediments, granite.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Napa Valley
summary: California's most famous AVA, north of San Francisco, renowned for rich, opulent Cabernet Sauvignon.
climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooler in the south (Carneros) thanks to San Pablo Bay fog.
soils: Over 30 soil series: volcanic on the mountains, alluvial fans on the valley floor.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Zinfandel.

name: Oregon
summary: Pacific Northwest state whose Willamette Valley is America's leading source of Burgundian-style Pinot Noir.
climate: Cool maritime, with wet winters and dry summers.
soils: Volcanic Jory soils, marine sedimentary Willakenzie soils and wind-blown loess.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay.

name: Mendoza
summary: Argentina's dominant region at the foot of the Andes, the world's home of Malbec, with high-altitude vineyards in the Uco Valley.
climate: Dry, sunny high desert (600–1,500 m) with a large diurnal range; irrigated from Andes snowmelt.
soils: Alluvial sands, gravels and limestone deposits.
typical_varietals: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda, Torrontés, Chardonnay.
